Chapter 3: The Slow Unfolding of Tyranny
You know, it’s tempting to think evil always shows up with alarms blaring—a sudden, dramatic moment you just can’t miss. But in Berlin, things didn’t happen all at once. Change crept in quietly, almost too slowly to notice at first.
Through the eyes of the ambassador—a man who loved history and paid attention to detail—everyday life in the city seemed to shift bit by bit. Each morning brought a new restriction, some fresh reason to be wary.
Laws were rewritten quietly, tucked away in the back pages of the newspapers. Suddenly, Jewish citizens couldn’t work in certain professions. Political opponents? They simply vanished, their names scrubbed from public memory. And the lively press that once thrived in Berlin? It turned into just another megaphone for the regime, full of empty praise for the so-called new order.
The ambassador did his best to sound the alarm. He wrote detailed reports, laying out every sign of repression he saw—hoping someone back home would listen. But in Washington, his warnings seemed to fall on deaf ears. Folks there mostly saw Germany’s problems as far away, nothing to do with them. Some even admired the country’s new strictness and order.
Inside the embassy, things weren’t any easier. Many on his staff were career diplomats, and they didn’t exactly welcome his different style. They doubted his common-sense approach and wondered if he really understood the job. For the ambassador, all the formalities and diplomatic games felt like a maze—he much preferred getting straight to the point.
As the regime’s grip tightened, the ambassador’s family felt the pressure too. Friends became nervous about stopping by the embassy, worried about being seen with Americans. His daughter, once the heart of every gathering, started to feel isolated. The Berlin they’d fallen in love with? It began to feel more like a cage, closing in around them.
There was one afternoon that really drove it home. The ambassador went to watch a parade meant to celebrate the regime. At first glance, the sidewalks were packed with cheering crowds—everyone’s face lit up with excitement. But he noticed the tension hiding just below the surface. How people kept glancing nervously over their shoulders. How conversations died the second officials passed by. That joy? It was just a mask, carefully worn to cover up the real fear underneath.
Slowly, the family realized they weren’t just watching history—they were living it. Being in Berlin was both a privilege and a heavy responsibility. They had the unique chance to witness these changes firsthand, but also the duty to speak out against injustice.
